Test whether prevalence is changing linearly over time

Source: R/test_trend.R
test_trend.Rd

Given the number of positives and the number tested at several timepoints (optionally at several sites per timepoint), fits a straight line to the measured prevalences and tests whether its slope differs from zero with the Cochran-Armitage trend test. Returns the estimated change in true prevalence per unit of time with its confidence interval, the p-value and whether the trend is significant. It is the analysis twin of design_trend().

Hypotheses (\(\beta\) is the slope of true prevalence):

"two.sided" (default)

H0: \(\beta = 0\) against H1: \(\beta \ne 0\).

"greater"

H0: \(\beta \le 0\) against H1: \(\beta > 0\) (an increasing trend).

"less"

H0: \(\beta \ge 0\) against H1: \(\beta < 0\) (a decreasing trend).

Usage

test_trend(
  x,
  n,
  time = NULL,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less"),
  sensitivity = 1,
  specificity = 1,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  icc = NULL
)

Arguments

x

Vector of whole-number counts of people who tested positive: one per timepoint, or one per site and timepoint (give the timepoint of each in time).

n

Vector of whole-number totals tested, the same length as x.

time

Numeric vector giving the timepoint of each value of x (for example calendar years or survey rounds). If NULL (default), 1, 2, ... is used, which only makes sense with one value per timepoint.

alternative

Direction of the test: "two.sided" (default), "greater" (increasing) or "less" (decreasing).

sensitivity

Diagnostic sensitivity in (0, 1]; default 1 (the test never misses a case).

specificity

Diagnostic specificity in (0, 1]; default 1 (the test never gives a false positive). sensitivity + specificity must exceed 1.

conf_level

Confidence level for the interval, in (0, 1); default 0.95. The significance level of the test is 1 - conf_level.

icc

Optional. Intra-cluster correlation, in [0, 1]. If NULL (default), it is estimated from the timepoints with two or more sites. Set to 0 for no clustering.

Value

A list with:

slope

Estimated change in true prevalence per unit of time.

ci_lower, ci_upper

Confidence interval for the slope; ci_upper is Inf for "greater" and ci_lower is -Inf for "less".

p_value

p-value for the chosen alternative.

reject

TRUE if p_value is below 1 - conf_level.

n_eff

Effective sample size, sum(n) / deff.

icc

ICC used: as supplied, or estimated from the data.

deff

Design effect used (1 with no clustering).

Details

Line. The counts are added up within each timepoint, giving \(X_j\) positives of \(N_j\) tested at time \(t_j\), and measured prevalence \(\hat p_j = X_j / N_j\). Each timepoint is weighted by its effective number tested, \(w_j = N_j / D_{eff}\). The slope is $$\hat\beta_{app} = \frac{\sum_j w_j (t_j - \bar t)\,\hat p_j} {\sum_j w_j (t_j - \bar t)^2},$$ where \(\bar t\) is the weighted mean time.

Test. With no trend every timepoint has the weighted mean prevalence \(\bar p\), and the slope has variance \(\bar p (1 - \bar p) / \sum_j w_j (t_j - \bar t)^2\). The z-statistic is the slope divided by its standard error (the Cochran-Armitage trend test). Without sites it gives the same p-value as R's prop.trend.test().

Interval. For a possible slope \(\beta\), take the line with that slope through \(\bar p\) at \(\bar t\), cut to [0, 1]; call its value at each timepoint \(f_j\). If that line were true, the slope would have variance \(V(\beta) = \sum_j w_j (t_j - \bar t)^2 f_j (1 - f_j) / (\sum_j w_j (t_j - \bar t)^2)^2\). The interval holds the slopes with \((\hat\beta_{app} - \beta)^2 \le z^2 V(\beta)\). At \(\beta = 0\) this is the test, so reject is TRUE exactly when 0 is outside the interval. It is matched to alternative: one-sided for "greater" and "less". The slope and its interval are divided by \(Se + Sp - 1\) to give the trend in true prevalence.

Design effect. It is \(1 + (n_w - 1) ICC\), where \(n_w = \sum n^2 / \sum n\) is the mean number of people per site, weighted by site size, and is applied to every timepoint. With icc = NULL, an ICC is estimated within each timepoint that has two or more sites (as in estimate_prevalence()), and the estimates are averaged; timepoints with one person per site, or with all negative or all positive, are skipped. With one site per timepoint there is nothing to estimate from, and a supplied icc is ignored with a warning.

References

Armitage, P. (1955) Tests for linear trends in proportions and frequencies. Biometrics 11(3), 375-386. doi:10.2307/3001775

Cochran, W. G. (1954) Some methods for strengthening the common chi-square tests. Biometrics 10(4), 417-451. doi:10.2307/3001616

Kish, L. (1965) Survey Sampling. Wiley. (Design effect.)

Rogan, W. J. & Gladen, B. (1978) Estimating prevalence from the results of a screening test. American Journal of Epidemiology 107(1), 71-76. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a112510

MMS-SD Study Design Workshop. https://mrc-ide.github.io/MMS-SD_workshop/

See also

design_trend()

Examples

# Five annual rounds, one survey per round
test_trend(x = c(5, 8, 9, 14, 17), n = rep(100, 5), time = 2019:2023)
#> $slope
#> [1] 0.03
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] 0.01096155
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 0.0482649
#> 
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.00205777
#> 
#> $reject
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 500
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 

# Two sites per round, ICC estimated from the data
test_trend(
  x    = c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 7, 10),
  n    = c(50, 45, 55, 50, 48, 52, 47, 51),
  time = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4)
)
#> $slope
#> [1] 0.04175961
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] 0.01363743
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 0.06858299
#> 
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.003665485
#> 
#> $reject
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 398
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 

# Imperfect diagnostic test, one-sided (a decline)
test_trend(x = c(20, 15, 11, 7), n = rep(120, 4), time = 1:4,
           alternative = "less", sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.97)
#> $slope
#> [1] -0.04118774
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] -Inf
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] -0.01705297
#> 
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.002550328
#> 
#> $reject
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 480
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#>
